At another I am the empirical I. Who is going to tell me I cannot? I, the lout, affirm myself as the lout I am. But ironically.
The most shameless insult ever inflicted upon God and man, an insult that would justify every curse of the synagogue, lies in the sive of the formula:
Our Stirner does not do that. He does not say: I, or God. Or perhaps he does. But he does it loutishly, not deceitfully.

As though one had wandered into a cheap cabaret led by a five-penny d’Annunzio. So he really does belong to the horrifying milieu in which I was trapped between 1912 and 1919. And I too was apparently good enough to be worked into the mixture.
Kluxen recognized him for what he was and immediately noticed the similarity between Däubler’s own existence and that of his African heroine. I was too naive.

Strange how Däubler was replaced by Haecker and Konrad Weiß. But all three of them—Däubler, Haecker, Weiß—were professional journalists. So this is what the figures of today’s pouvoir spirituel, spiritual authority, actually look like in concrete reality.
The sociology of intellectuals in the age of capitalism.
Second disillusionment of yesterday: the photograph of G. Bernanos in Le Figaro, July 1939. So he too has firmly established himself as a professional man of letters.
A very fine gentleman as well.
Authentic Oberammergau in the Hollywood of the Coop. Int. Int.
The devastating feeling of having been deceived.
No longer even capable of using irony as a form of self-defense.
The defeated man in someone else’s just war.
How horrifying are Maritain’s whorish enticements in Humanisme intégral (1936):
“The theologians and moralists explain to us under what conditions the physical means of war are just. It is not their task to open new doors to violence.”
But, Monsieur Maritain, that is their effect!
“Once the doors have been opened, however, they justify whatever can be justified.”
Yes indeed. That is exactly what it says on p. 262.
Apparently it is not their task to close the doors to violence either. They justify whatever can be justified.
The doctrine of the just war is exceptionally well suited to this. It already did the same thing regarding long-range crossbows and projectiles at the Second Lateran Council in 1139.
And today it does the same thing regarding the atomic bomb and the other new means of annihilation.
The just war means: the enemy is stripped of his rights, while the just side authorizes itself to do what is necessary.
The result is the transformation of war between states—that is, war governed by international law—into a war that is colonial war and civil war at the same time. This is logical and irrefutable.
War becomes world civil war. It stops being war between states.
(I am suffocating beneath the fraud of the ideology of world civil war.
Does no human ear hear my voice?)
Poor dispenser of justice that you are.
The poor Germans today are really the orphans of Leviathan.
All I can still do is pray:
Lead me back to my father,
Let what belongs to me be returned to me,
so that You may be glorified in Your justice.
Whoever ruined his longing for some good of this world …
We Germans are being pushed beyond the line.
Into the condition of the peaceless and outlawed.

The disinherited of Leviathan. Those whom Leviathan has spat out. We, who possess the great possibility of advancing from the relative beyond into which we are being pushed toward the absolute beyond: the overcoming of the world itself.
“Stricter than art” are “the measures and proportions of concrete law.”
This belongs with the Hölderlin quotation in The Three Types of Juristic Thought, p. 17.
Whoever falsifies his mission becomes, by that very fact, the idol of his age. And he becomes its idol precisely to the degree that he falsifies his mission.
Only when he becomes the idol of the whole world do we arrive at the son of wickedness and the public triumph, before the whole world, of the mysterium iniquitatis: the mystery of lawlessness.
You wanted, in Kierkegaard’s sense, to “deceive” these arch-deceivers into the truth.
And then there are the extraordinary things in Kierkegaard’s answer to the question:
May a person allow himself to be beaten to death for the truth?
Written at the end of 1847, at the same time as the Communist Manifesto.
The person with enough strength to give his age the passion required to beat him to death.
There too we find more about the preachers of repentance of our age.
“To be the great preacher of repentance means to be beaten to death.”
Bernanos seems to have sensed something of this when he spoke in Geneva. Yet the experts on Kierkegaard apparently do not notice it.
Continue your afterword to The Concept of Irony!
If you can erase eighteen hundred years, it should not be difficult for you to erase the final eighteen years that have passed since that afterword.
Or do you want to offer the age you despise so much the miserable spectacle of repentance-preachers fighting among themselves?
Seen through Kierkegaard’s eyes, this is surely one degree more pathetic than the officially approved preacher in a church pulpit.
To Günther Krauss, who wrote that he could not really call Kleist’s women Marian:
Kleist’s women are, first of all, not “ladies” like Goethe’s Iphigenia. That removes the main obstacle to connecting Kleist with the Virgin Mother.
Mary is the woman among women.
And is the Maid of Orléans really not Kleistian?
Once the Ecce ancilla—“Behold the handmaid”—is properly understood, the whole problem appears differently. And the Ecce ancilla is surely the center of a Marian view of history.
Shakespeare, on the other hand, is in no sense Marian. But Annette, the wise-foolish virgin, belongs with Kleist.
Is it not sad that the two never met?
Though this would have been one of those encounters that German circumstances never permit.
What does it actually mean when Sohm says that law is tied to the past?
Is this an absolutization of nullum crimen—no crime without a prior law? Or what is it?
With Hobbes, the meaning, and its connection with nominalism, is immediately clear.
Is it equally clear with Sohm?
The accelerator of accelerators against his own will.
Sohm’s touching error: law protects the weak.
Customary law, by contrast, supposedly serves the strong.
